Abstract Quiet quitting is a fairly recent labor phenomenon, but it has spread to various organizational settings, as it exposes important problems for the effectiveness of companies, as well as for workers and their job stability. This paper aimed to analyze the main characteristics of publications on quiet quitting from a bibliometric analysis from 2016 to 2024. The process began with a literature review in the Scopus database, through which 1210 scientific articles were identified as the basis for the bibliometric analysis; likewise, a cartographic analysis was performed with VOSviewer. This software made it possible to identify and trace the interconnection and collaboration networks between authors, countries, institutions, and keywords, providing information on research activity related to this labor phenomenon. The scientific production was analyzed and the following sub-areas (clusters) were identified from the studies examined: quiet quitting, sustainability, and social capital. The results obtained showed that the year with the highest productivity was 2024, and the thematic area of business, management, and accounting presented the highest number of studies on quitting. It is concluded that quiet quitting is related to employee engagement, labor turnover management, and organizational culture. It also highlights that it is necessary to pay attention to employee behavior, since when this occurs, organizations can obtain information that will allow them to confront and mitigate the negative effects of quiet quitting. In this sense, the strategies applied should focus on fostering a more humane and resilient work environment. Keywords: quiet quitting, bibliometric analysis, organizational psychology, human capital, working conditions 1. Introduction Globalization, as an economic, geopolitical, social, and technological phenomenon, has allowed the establishment of exponential communication, marked by interdependence between nations, which has led to the unification of markets, technological impact, and various changes in social and cultural aspects (Torres & Bosio, 2020). At the organizational level, one of the guidelines that has driven the most significant changes in the development of nations has been the conception of "intelligent companies" (Lavorato & Piedepalumbo, 2023; Aggarwal et al., 2022). Within these organizations, work relationships play a major role, in which human resources managers have the purpose of maintaining a harmonious, balanced, and highly productive work environment that promotes the practice of critical-reflective thinking (Erdoğan, 2020; Cabanilla et al., 2022). In this sense, in modern organizations that direct their labor policies to establish sustainable motivational conditions, detecting personnel needs becomes a continuous and constant task (Jose et al., 2021; Piwowar-Sulej, 2021). Thus, the management team of each organization associates a harmonious work environment with high productivity, which, in turn, is reflected in the profitability and sustainability of the company (Philipp, 2020). Currently, the vast majority of entrepreneurial structures that produce goods or provide services on a large scale have experienced significant and unforeseen changes in the behavior of some workers who, due to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, were driven to work from home in an almost improvised manner (Babapour et al., 2022). This change in work methodology has been framed in the so-called "remote work or teleworking", which at the beginning had an obvious impact on people because it was not planned in time, but as the whole context developed, it triggered a new work trend worldwide (Barriga et al., 2021; Verick et al., 2021). (2026) 2 Due to the progressive changes in the post-pandemic period, several companies proceeded to reincorporate personnel into their jobs, and in some cases detected difficulties in performing tasks adequately (Türkeș & Vuță, 2022). Consequently, some workers presented personal and family arguments for not returning to face-to-face mode, while a significant number expressed their desire to withdraw permanently from the organization (Qureshi et al., 2023). In this order of ideas, studies carried out in 2023 have indicated that many workers have difficulties associating or relating with the rest of the work team after returning from remote work (Lal et al., 2023; De Vincenzi et al., 2022). Such a situation has been reflected in the trend of a drop in the efficiency of collaborative work, which has generated a limitation in the expected organizational scope (Tiernan et al., 2023). This has forced Human Resources (HR) managers to implement new bidirectional and multidirectional communication channels that allow each member to express their disagreements and receive support (Rangaswamy et al., 2023). However, the low level of activation, low expectations, and poor satisfaction of some workers to proactively develop the functions inherent to their position in the internal spaces of the organization are still latent (Radu et al., 2023). On the other hand, the sociocultural differences present in Latin America have a significant influence on the sustainable development of labor relations (Cerón-Anaya et al., 2023; Rodríguez-Del Pino & Aguado-Hernández, 2023). Perceptions, beliefs, and value schemes in each society show differences in the behavior of the people living in the regions that make up each country. These elements have become determining factors that intervene in the conception of a stable, proactive, and comfortable work environment (Karimi et al., 2023). Consequently, some specialists have pointed out that the effects of the post-pandemic have contributed to creating a silent behavior in many workers of productive age, in which low participation, weak collaboration, and poor communication have given way to the so-called "quiet quitting" (Mahand & Caldwell, 2023; Hamilton, 2023). It is understood, then, that the phenomenon of quiet quitting has emerged as a complex response to changes in the post-pandemic work environment, showing how working conditions, organizational policies and sociocultural differences influence employee commitment and motivation. Organizations, especially in Latin America, face the challenge of adapting to the new expectations of workers, who seek a work-life balance and demand more flexible and sustainable work environments. This situation requires human resources managers to develop innovative strategies that address the emotional and cultural aspects of teams, strengthening cohesion and job satisfaction. The implementation of effective communication and emotional support policies becomes critical to overcome the barriers created by quiet quitting and promote a work environment that fosters a sense of belonging and proactivity. As companies navigate these challenges, the role of labor relations is being redefined, moving towards a model that prioritizes the integral well-being of workers, which is crucial for organizational sustainability and competitiveness in an increasingly interconnected world. Amid this reality, organizational psychology is used as an aid for the performance of companies, since through the motivation of personnel it is possible to improve the quality of life of workers, as well as their well-being, efficiency, and productivity in the workplace. It also provides the necessary help to efficiently and effectively solve the problems and obstacles that arise in the work environment, while providing the right tools to raise employee morale and care for their psychological state (Al-Abri et al., 2021). Accordingly, the following research questions were established in this study: 1. How has the evolution been in terms of the number of articles published on quiet quitting? 2. How are publications distributed in different countries? 3. Who are the most prominent authors in the professional literature on quiet quitting in terms of several publications and citations? 4. What are the bibliometric data of the studies reviewed? From this perspective, this study aimed to analyze the main characteristics of publications on quiet quitting based on a bibliometric analysis. 1.1. Related work. Quiet quitting is a modern concept characterized by a progressive detachment of the worker from work goals or objectives (Galanis et al., 2023; Gabelaia & Bagociunaite, 2024). It is an attitudinal philosophy associated with the behavior of certain people in the workplace, which leads them, even when they are working in person, to show a mental, spiritual, and even emotional detachment, so that they do the minimum necessary to justify their work (Kang et al., 2023; Alaql et al., 2023). At the structural level, quiet quitting has become a point of organizational attention in both governmental sectors and in consortiums that operate with private capital. This attitude is reflected in labor performance and the increase in costs for the maintenance of labor, both indirect and direct (Galanis et al., 2023; Ng & Stanton, 2023). Similarly, recent studies associate this tendency with various factors, including those of sociocultural origins, such for example, values, beliefs, customs, and traditions (Iso-Ahola & Baumeister, 2023). Faced with this situation, companies have resorted to organizational psychology as a way to understand and provide the necessary help to workers who may present some kind of labor or personal dissatisfaction. This area of psychology is an https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj León-Velarde et al. (2026) 3 interdisciplinary field of action, whose objective is to understand the phenomena that could be generated at the business level, which occur around a series of aspects related to the well-being of the person (Schein, 1982; De Lara et al., 2011). In this sense, Zuluaga & Quintero (2022) point out that it is of utmost importance to identify in time the factors that affect working conditions and their results since it is possible to provide workers with the necessary support to achieve mental stability and maintain or increase their productivity. Therefore, understanding the reasons behind the intentions of a possible resignation is extremely important both for organizations and for the work performed by the organizational psychologist. The intentions of an employee to leave or not to leave the company can be influenced by both environmental factors and individual differences. Thus, Treglown et al. (2018) demonstrated that individual difference variables and workplace factors play an important role in explaining why employees wish to leave their organization. In conclusion, the literature reviewed highlights the importance of addressing the phenomenon of quiet quitting as a growing trend that affects not only individual productivity, but also organizational performance in general. The progressive disengagement of employees from their work goals poses a significant challenge to the public and private sectors, due to increased turnover costs and decreased engagement in the work environment. In addition, studies highlight that this behavior may have deep roots in sociocultural factors, suggesting that the organizational response should consider a variety of strategies tailored to the cultural context of employees. On the other hand, organizational psychology intervention emerges as a key resource to mitigate quitting and promote job stability. By identifying the factors that affect employee satisfaction and well-being, organizations can implement measures that strengthen the sense of belonging and reduce resignation intentions. The literature highlights the relevance of an early assessment of working conditions and individual factors, which may influence the employee's decision to stay or not in the company. This integrative vision allows not only to improve talent retention, but also to foster a positive and sustainable work environment. 2. Materials and Methods In this study, bibliometric analysis techniques were used to examine the existing literature on quiet quitting at the organizational level. 2.1. Data collection The search process was performed on 2024, and 1210 records were found in the Scopus database. The data collection procedure began with downloading bibliographic data of relevant publications from Scopus. Then, the data were cleaned by eliminating duplicates and verifying the relevance of each publication. Subsequently, the publications were assigned codes according to subject categories, authors, affiliations, and other relevant attributes. 2.2. Research design Bibliometric analysis allows the evaluation of scientific production through the analysis of publications, citations, and other quantitative indicators (Flores-Fernández & Aguilera-Eguía, 2019; García-Villara & García-Santos, 2021). The search for relevant documents was determined by several criteria, among which were the following: time, type of document, thematic focus and language. The Scopus database, selected for its broad scope and recognition in the academic community (Sandoval, 2020), was used exclusively for the compilation of the studies. The period of analysis covered publications from 2016 to 2024, both in English and Spanish, focused on the phenomenon of silent resignation. In terms of document types, the review included various types of documents, such as journal articles, reviews, conference proceedings, books, and book chapters. 2.3. Quantitative research design The search strategy was designed to capture all relevant publications on quiet quitting. To this end, combinations of keywords and specific search terms were used, employing Boolean operators to refine and expand the searches as needed; these were set up as follows: (TITLE-ABS-KEY ("Quiet Quitting") OR ("organizational psychology") OR ("Job disengagement") OR ("human capital") OR ("working conditions") OR ("Professional disinterest") OR ("Gradual withdrawal")) AND PUBYEAR > 2003 AND PUBYEAR < 2025. The data analysis was carried out in several stages. First, a descriptive analysis was carried out, which included counting the total number of publications per year, identifying the most productive authors, and the institutions with the greatest scientific production on the topic. Second, a network analysis was performed to examine co-authorship and co-citation, identifying collaborations between authors and institutions and relationships between jointly cited papers and authors. Finally, a content analysis focused on keywords and titles of publications, analyzing frequencies and trends to identify emerging themes and research patterns over time. For data analysis and visualization, VOSviewer software was used to analyze co-authorship and co-citation networks. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj León-Velarde et al. (2026) 4 It is important to note the limitations of the study, such as the dependence on the coverage and precision of Scopus; the restriction of the analysis to publications in English and Spanish, which may exclude relevant studies in other languages; and the limitation of the analysis to a specific period, which may not capture broader historical trends. Regarding ethical considerations, the study respected the intellectual property and copyrights of the publications analyzed. The original data were not manipulated or altered, and the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis were ensured. 3. Results and discussion The search began in 2016 and found a total of 1210 articles on quiet quitting of employees; however, although the use of the term does not date back to that year, there was always a desire in the scientific community to study the attitude of workers to work situations that were not to their liking. This attitude was called, in studies prior to the period indicated, “turnover intention”, which basically referred to the intention of a worker to remain in an organization or leave it (Pienaar et al., 2007; Bothma and Roodt, 2013). The interest of these authors, among many others, in knowing the reason for a worker's “intention” to leave his or her job was what motivated us to extend the temporal range of the study and, thus, to verify its use in the literature. However, it was in 2022 when Creely (2022) used the expression in his social network TikTok, alluding to the need to set limits on abusive colleagues and bosses. Subsequently, the publication of articles referring to quiet quitting was related to disengagement from work commitments (Bhatt et al., 2024). CLUSTER 1: Quiet quitting The labor world was used to the usual resignations expressed through writings and traditional procedures used by employees; however, nowadays there is another type of resignation, which is known by the term "silent resignation" or quiet quitting. This is defined as the secret or covert departure without the knowledge of the organization, which causes continuous job vacancies and sudden departures (Alami et al., 2024). Domingue et al. (2024) point out that this expression became a trend through the social network TikTok in July 2022; from that moment on, it spread as a method of employee resistance to the increasing demands of their workplaces, which increasingly endangered their family, social and leisure time. For the authors, silent resignation consists of refraining from going beyond the demands of the workplace, limiting oneself only to the tasks described for one's position. In essence, quiet quitting refers to employees limiting their actions to their specific roles, without displaying enthusiasm or dedication. Therefore, it is crucial to understand the underlying causes of employee resignations and how they can be proactively prevented. This trend has been observed in many countries, particularly among younger employees, and could have a detrimental impact on organizational culture (Boy & Sürmeli, 2023). Bhatt et al. (2024) argue that quitting silently arises as a deliberate response to a toxic work environment, the triggers of which are related to certain factors, including low pay and limited development opportunities. It is not an abrupt decision, but a gradual accumulation of dissatisfaction. This delicate labor situation should lead the employer to know and understand the needs of its personnel, to foster an adequate work environment where both organizational and individual employee growth prevails. In this sense, they should build trust by actively listening and adapting to the concerns of their employees, creating human resources policies that can improve the performance and commitment of the staff, thus contributing to the overall success and productivity of the company (Alami et al., 2024; Suhendar et al., 2023). 3.9. CLUSTER 2: Sustainability. Organizational culture refers to the set of significant values, beliefs, and understandings that the members of an organization have in common, which supports decision-making and other business activities. In the organizational culture, it is necessary to prioritize teamwork and solidarity, so that there is a shift in focus from results to synergy. To achieve the longed- for sustainable success, solidarity among members is more effective than immediate results (Campton et al., 2023). However, quiet quitting, which has been observed in various countries, particularly among younger employees, could negatively affect the quality of health care by promoting a toxic organizational culture (Suhendar et al., 2023). Hence, there is a need for structural changes in the healthcare industry, including policies that address both employee well-being and the structural problems that lead to burnout and retention. When there is a healthy approach, and a culture of retention and commitment in healthcare institutions to address quiet quitting, there will also be successful management and a sustainable future in that area (Domingue et al., 2024). Similarly, to address silent resignation, it is necessary to reflect on work cultures, emphasizing greater autonomy in the way work is performed (when necessary), and, consequently, reevaluating employment contracts (Bhatt et al., 2024; Campton et al., 2023). In addition, the studies analyzed stress the need to promote a positive work culture and development opportunities for employees, creating human resources policies that successfully contribute to the sustainability of the company (Suhendar et al., 2023). 3.10. CLUSTER 3: Social capital This cluster includes elements such as competitive advantage, financial capital, efficiency, and psychological capital, all of which are present in the business or organizational world. Social capital favors the generation of future benefits for organizations, due to its importance in building trust, business success, and productive efficiency. Likewise, social capital affects https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj León-Velarde et al. (2026) 10 the people who are part of the companies, allows the generation of competitive advantages, and in general, improves the operation and results of the companies. In this sense, the term "social capital" is related to quiet quitting, since organizations must invest in building trust in their personnel, which is why a considerable number of companies worldwide are transforming their work environments to provide a more familiar environment for their employees. If these small details are not handled properly, it is possible to generate high turnover rates and hinder organizational growth. Hence, people must perform a job according to their attitudes, skills, and interests, which allows them to maintain their well-being and productivity (Bhatt et al., 2024). For Campton et al. (2023), there are cultural and generational influences in the Asian labor market, which should lead companies to reconsider different communication channels and create open and safe forums to generate discussions about work culture with their workers. Also, to address the emergence of quiet quitting, Asian companies should conduct employee surveys to measure and collect data on employee morale, workload, commitment, and organizational loyalty. Finally, organizations should orient their policies towards greater flexibility and openness in communication to retain younger generations entering the labor market. Another highly significant aspect is addressed by Lu et al. (2023), who, using social exchange theory, demonstrated the connection between employee well-being, psychological empowerment, work-related factors, burnout, and the intention to quit quietly. They further showed that employee well-being reduces the intention to quit quietly, while job burnout increases it. Additionally, psychological empowerment positively influences both the relationship between job burnout and the intention to quit quietly, and the relationship between employee well-being and the intention to quit quietly. 4. Conclusions The bibliometric analysis allowed for analyzing the main characteristics of publications on quiet quitting in the period between 2016 and 2024. This type of study has not been explored as a topic of importance in the development of the area, so it is recommended to carry it out, especially due to the labor reality currently presented by various countries, which is characterized by the presence of a fairly young population. The analysis identified 1210 scientific articles according to their authors, affiliation, year, thematic area, countries of publication, categories, and journals indexed in Scopus. As a result, it was possible to establish that the year 2024 was the year with the highest productivity with 120 studies; this number of papers shows its importance as a social and labor phenomenon. Moreover, this peak reached during 2024 reveals the critical moment when this phenomenon caught the attention of the scientific community because of changes experienced in the labor market, because of the COVID-19 pandemic or because of new labor policies. As for the countries with the highest scientific production on silent resignation, the United States stood out with 485 papers, followed by China, the United Kingdom and India, with more than 60 papers each. The presence of these countries demonstrates that silent resignation is a highly relevant aspect in different socioeconomic and cultural contexts, which favors the understanding of the phenomenon through varied and comparative perspectives. Likewise, the leadership of the USA in terms of published studies demonstrates the importance of the topic in the North American context, due to the specific characteristics of the labor market and the organizational culture of that country. The area of Business, Management and Accounting showed the highest number of publications referring to the topic analyzed, followed by Social Sciences and Medicine. The most prominent authors in the study of silent resignation were Galanis, P., Katsiroumpa, A., Vraka, I., and Moisoglou, I. from the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens. Also, three sub- clusters were also identified: quiet quitting, sustainability, and social capital. It should be noted that silent resignation has become an active field for the scientific community due to the recent characteristics of the labor market because of the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as the development and empowerment of Generation Z. This generational group warrants special attention, as their negative experiences during the pandemic, coupled with a strong preference for work-life balance, have resulted in a more relaxed approach towards the demands of their work environment. Among other factors, working conditions, job security, perceived career development opportunities, effective organizational commitment and perceived organizational support on job burnout and well-being determine the intention to quit, especially among Chinese Generation Z employees. They have been known to reject intense competition, preferring a more relaxed lifestyle (Xueyun et al., 2023). Finally, it was established that quiet quitting at the organizational level is linked to employee commitment, labor turnover, and organizational culture. Based on the relationship between these elements, it is necessary to consider the behavior of employees, so that organizations can address and mitigate the negative effects of silent resignation. Therefore, it is necessary to implement a more humane and resilient work environment, as well as to apply the most relevant strategies to deal with this phenomenon. JSON: Name: quiet_quitting_predictive_pipeline Title: Supervised machine learning prediction of employee quiet quitting intention using organizational, psychological, and bibliometric-derived features Short Hypothesis: Augmenting standard employee demographic, job, and psychological features with bibliometric-derived organizational knowledge features increases predictive AUC for quiet quitting intention by at least 0.05 on held-out test data. Related Work: Prior work on quiet quitting has produced: (1) descriptive and conceptual studies that define and qualitatively characterize quiet quitting and its drivers (e.g., burnout, work–life balance, toxic work culture); (2) psychometric efforts that develop and validate measurement instruments (quiet quitting scales, burnout/well-being scales); and (3) bibliometric mappings that identify thematic clusters (engagement, sustainability, social capital) and geographic/disciplinary concentrations. Limitations across these streams: most empirical studies are cross-sectional and correlational (no predictive claims or temporal validation); sample sizes are often small or single-organization; few studies apply formal supervised-learning or benchmarked predictive models; organizational-level knowledge (e.g., institutional research activity or sectoral bibliometric signals) is not used as predictive input; external and temporal generalization is rarely tested; and model interpretability and calibration receive limited attention. No established baseline exists that jointly uses psychological, job, demographic, and bibliometric-derived organizational features in a predictive, multi-country, longitudinal evaluation. Abstract: This project builds a validated predictive pipeline to forecast employees' quiet quitting intention using supervised machine learning on integrated employee-level, organizational, and bibliometric-derived features. The problem addressed is early identification of employees likely to adopt quiet quitting behaviors so organizations can prioritize interventions. We propose to collect longitudinal survey panels (psychological scales, job characteristics, demographics) and link those records to firm-level metadata and bibliometric-derived organizational indicators (research activity, topical signals related to engagement/sustainability/social capital). The main contribution is a reproducible benchmark: preprocessed datasets, baseline models (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, neural network), interpretable feature attributions, and ablation analyses quantifying the incremental value of bibliometric-derived features. Expected outcomes are (1) calibrated models with demonstrated out-of-sample performance; (2) quantification of predictive lift from bibliometric features; and (3) public experimental protocol for future comparative studies. The pipeline will enable evidence-based prioritization of organizational diagnostics and future causal intervention trials. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary longitudinal employee panel: N = 6,000 employees across 100 firms in four countries (USA, UK, China, India); baseline survey + 6-month follow-up; labels = quiet quitting intention at 6 months measured by validated Quiet Quitting Scale threshold (binary) and continuous score. (B) External validation set: N = 2,000 employees from 30 different firms not in training set. (C) Public auxiliary data: firm metadata (size, industry NAICS code, remote-work policy), firm-level bibliometric-derived features computed from institutional publications and public organizational profiles over preceding 5 years (publication volume, topical prevalence scores for engagement/sustainability/social capital via term-frequency vectors), and regional labor-market indicators. Feature sets: demographic (age, gender, tenure, education), job (role, hours, contract type, remote fraction), psychological (burnout, well-being, psychological empowerment), organizational metadata, bibliometric-derived features. Baselines: (1) logistic regression with L2, (2) penalized logistic (elastic net), (3) random forest, (4) XGBoost, (5) feedforward neural network. Model training: nested stratified 5-fold CV on training firms, hyperparameter tuning via grid/random search; calibration via isotonic regression on validation fold; final evaluation on held-out test firms and external validation set. Evaluation metrics: AUC-ROC (primary), AUPRC, accuracy, F1, precision@k (k=5% top risk), Brier score, calibration plots, decision-curve analysis. Statistical tests: DeLong test for AUC differences, paired bootstrap for metric CIs. Ablation studies: (A) remove bibliometric-derived features vs full model; (B) remove psychological features vs full model; (C) train on country A, test on country B to measure cross-country generalization; (D) temporal generalization: train on t0→t1, test t1→t2 if available. Robustness checks: label-noise sensitivity (flip 10%/20% labels), class-imbalance handling (SMOTE, class-weighting). Interpretability: global feature importance (SHAP), per-group explanations. Required preprocessing: categorical encoding (one-hot or target encoding), numeric scaling, multiple imputation for missing data (MICE), and pipeline invariants for deployment. Success criterion: full model AUC improvement ≥0.05 over baseline using only demographic+job+psychological features on held-out test set. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self-report bias and label noise in survey-based quiet quitting measures; nonresponse and attrition in longitudinal panels causing selection bias; cultural and language differences affecting scale validity across countries; limited external validity to industries or regions not sampled; bibliometric-derived features may not map uniformly to private-sector firms (few publications for SMEs) producing sparse or noisy organizational signals; temporal drift in predictors and labels reducing long-term model usefulness; privacy and data governance constraints limiting feature availability or sample size; class imbalance if quiet quitting prevalence is low leading to unreliable estimates; potential confounding between firm-level and individual-level predictors complicating causal interpretation; compute and storage limits for large-scale hyperparameter sweeps or ensembles in resource-constrained environments.
